Nice Classification 13th Edition (2026): Class Changes That Affect Your China Filing

China adopted the 13th edition of the Nice Classification with effect from 1 January 2026, and CNIPA has adjusted its table of similar goods and services accordingly. If your specification was written against the 12th edition, some of its items now sit in a different class.

The 1 January 2026 Cutover

China adopted the 13th edition (2026 text) of the Nice Classification with effect from 1 January 2026. Applications filed before that date continue to be examined under the 12th edition; the version in force on the filing date governs how goods and services are classified. That single cutover date is the fact to build a 2026 filing checklist around.

Nice classes are the international skeleton, but in China the working document is CNIPA's own classification of similar goods and services, which has been adjusted on the basis of the 13th edition. The table is what examiners use when they assess whether goods are similar, and it is more granular than the class headings. A filing prepared from an old class list can therefore be wrong even when the class number itself looks right.

Check the version, not just the class number. Before you reuse a specification from an earlier filing, confirm which edition it was written against and re-read the current CNIPA table for the exact item wording. Where the official text is unclear, ask your agent to check the current announcements and rules rather than assume continuity.

Goods That Moved Class

The 13th edition moves several everyday items between classes. These are the changes that most often catch out a portfolio that was filed years earlier and is now being extended or refreshed.

GoodsFromToNote
Spectacles and accessories: lenses, frames, sunglasses, contact lensesClass 9Class 10Smart glasses remain in Class 9
Electrically heated clothing, including heated socksClass 11Class 25Now classified with clothing
Emergency and rescue vehicles: fire engines, lifeboats and similarClass 9Class 12Now classified with vehicles
Buttercream and cream cakesClass 29Class 30Now classified with bakery and confectionery goods

The spectacles change is the one with the widest reach: eyewear brands that built a Class 9 portfolio may now need Class 10 coverage, while smart-glasses products stay where they were. Do not treat the whole eyewear category as having moved. Read the item wording, keep the smart-glasses exception in mind, and review pending applications as well as registrations when you map the gap.

New and Split Entries

Two further changes are additions and splits rather than transfers. Class 42 gains artificial intelligence as a service (AIaaS), giving a dedicated home for a service that previously had to be squeezed into broader computer and software items. Applicants offering AI platforms, model hosting or machine-learning services should check whether the new item gives a cleaner specification than the general software wording they used before.

Essential oils in Class 3 are split by intended use. Rather than a single catch-all item, classification now turns on what the oil is for, for example a cosmetic or fragrancing purpose versus another use. The practical consequence is that the wording of a Class 3 specification has to state the purpose, because the same product can fall under different items depending on how it is described and marketed.

For both entries, the discipline is the same: describe the actual goods or services, then find the current item, rather than copying a generic phrase from an old form and hoping the examiner will map it for you.

What the Change Does Not Do

Classification changes do not, by themselves, rewrite earlier filings. An application is examined under the edition in force on its filing date, which is why the 1 January 2026 line matters: a pre-cutover application stays on the 12th edition, and a post-cutover filing uses the 13th. A pending application is not automatically reclassified because the table later changed.

What the change does affect is everything you file or extend afterwards: new applications, later designations, renewals where the specification is revisited, and the scope you choose for defensive filings. It also affects how you read similarity. CNIPA's adjusted table of similar goods and services can group items differently from the older table, so a conflict analysis prepared under the 12th edition should be re-run where it involves a moved item.

Confirm the transitional rules officially. This article states the classification changes and the general filing-date principle; it does not set out a detailed transitional regime for pending cases or existing registrations. Where the position matters to a live filing, rely on CNIPA's current announcements and rules rather than a third-party summary.

A 2026 Filing Checklist

A short checklist keeps a 2026 filing programme clean:

  1. Confirm the applicable edition from the filing date, and record it in the file.
  2. Re-read the current CNIPA table for every item, including sub-class wording, instead of reusing a specification from an earlier portfolio.
  3. Re-map moved goods such as eyewear, heated clothing, rescue vehicles, buttercream and cream cakes, and check whether a new class is needed or the smart-glasses exception applies.
  4. Use the new and split items where they fit: AI as a service in Class 42, and purpose-specific wording for essential oils in Class 3.
  5. Refresh defensive and watch scopes so that monitoring covers the classes goods actually moved into, not only the classes they left.
  6. Re-run similarity searches for any conflict analysis prepared under the 12th edition, and update agent templates and filing checklists.

For the full class framework see our China trademark classes guide and registration guide. Where an item's placement is genuinely uncertain, ask for a written check against the current official text before filing.

Sources and Caveats

Basis: Nice Classification, 13th edition (2026 text), as adopted in China from 1 January 2026; CNIPA adjustments to its table of similar goods and services based on the 13th edition; the class transfers, the Class 42 AI-as-a-service addition and the purpose-based split of essential oils described above. Item wording and transitional practice should be confirmed against CNIPA's current announcements, rules and classification table before filing. This is general information, not legal advice.
